title: Blind spots: Examining political advertising misinformation and how U.S. news media hold political actors accountable
screen_reason: Abstract-only record of a multi-method study whose stated first contribution is 'to quantify the prevalence of inaccuracies in political advertising'. It gives a share of items (paid political TV ads aired in the 2008 US general election) that contained at least one inaccuracy according to FactCheck.org and PolitiFact ratings, i.e. items judged against an external fact-checking ground truth, with the aired-ad universe as denominator: CONTENT. A second share is given for evaluated claims. Both values are stated only as approximations ('just under 30%', 'more than three out of four'), so both rows are value_kind=range_not_point.

estimates.measure_type: % of paid political television ads aired in the 2008 US general election that contained at least one inaccuracy
estimates.denominator: All English-language paid political ads that aired on television during the 2008 US general election (count not stated in the abstract)
estimates.definition: The ad contained at least one inaccuracy, based on the ratings of FactCheck.org and PolitiFact.com
estimates.misinfo_def: "inaccuracies" in political advertising, operationalised as "at least one inaccuracy based upon the ratings of FactCheck.org and PolitiFact.com"
estimates.n: Not reported in the abstract (universe = all English-language paid political TV ads aired in the 2008 general election)
estimates.source_quote: Of all the English-language paid political ads that aired on television during the 2008 general election, just under 30% contained at least one inaccuracy based upon the ratings of FactCheck.org and PolitiFact.com.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Ratings published by FactCheck.org and PolitiFact.com, applied to the ads by the author via a content analysis; no coder-reliability statistics are given in the abstract
estimates.moderator_quote: This figure, however, is likely a gross under representation of the prevalence of inaccuracies in political ads from 2008 because most of the ads (70%) were never evaluated by these purportedly elite fact-checkers.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR - CEILING ARTEFACT: the denominator is every aired English-language paid political ad, but the numerator can only be drawn from the ~30% of ads the fact-checkers actually rated (the abstract says 70% were never evaluated). The author says so explicitly and calls the figure 'likely a gross under representation'. The 30% therefore behaves as a lower bound set by fact-checker coverage, not as an unbiased prevalence. Value is approximate ('just under 30%'), hence range_not_point with an empty value_pct; if the review's convention is to record the nearest stated number, 30 is the ceiling of the stated range, not a verbatim point estimate. Only the abstract was available, so the exact ad count and any coder reliability could not be recovered.

estimates.measure_type: % of the political-ad claims actually evaluated by fact-checkers that had some degree of inaccuracy
estimates.value_raw: more than three out of four of the evaluated claims
estimates.denominator: Claims within 2008 political television ads that were evaluated by FactCheck.org / PolitiFact.com (the abstract says only ~30% of ads were ever evaluated); count not stated
estimates.definition: The evaluated claim was rated as having some degree of inaccuracy
estimates.misinfo_def: "some degree of inaccuracy" in the ratings of FactCheck.org and PolitiFact.com
estimates.n: Not reported in the abstract (claims evaluated by the two fact-checkers)
estimates.source_quote: Among ads assessed, however, more than three out of four of the evaluated claims had some degree of inaccuracy.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: FactCheck.org and PolitiFact.com ratings of individual claims within the ads; selection of which claims to check was the fact-checkers' own
estimates.moderator_quote: This figure, however, is likely a gross under representation of the prevalence of inaccuracies in political ads from 2008 because most of the ads (70%) were never evaluated by these purportedly elite fact-checkers.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR - SELECTION: this denominator is fact-checker-selected claims, i.e. claims someone already thought worth checking, so the >75% is a within-selected-set rate and is not a prevalence of anything. Flagged borderline and denom_selection=curated for that reason; it is the natural candidate to drop if the review restricts to unselected denominators. It is NOT within_misinfo_content (the checked set is not a misinformation-only corpus), but it is close to that spirit. Value is approximate ('more than three out of four'), hence range_not_point.

missed_or_uncertain: Only the abstract was available, and it is a long dissertation-style abstract with no tables, so no exact counts, no N, no coder reliability and no confidence intervals could be recovered; the two rows are both approximations. Not extracted: (1) '70% [of ads] were never evaluated by these purportedly elite fact-checkers' - a fact-checker-coverage statistic, not a misinformation share, though it is recorded in both rows' moderator_quote because it bounds the first estimate. (2) 'ads containing at least one inaccuracy aired twice as often on television as the ads that were never evaluated' - a ratio of airing frequency, not a share with a denominator; note that if airing counts were available this would be the paper's exposure-weighted result, which the full text may report as a share (worth checking if the full text is ever obtained). (3) 'nearly half of their [political interest supporters'] spending was in the last weeks of the election' - a spending share, not a misinformation share. (4) Statements that inaccuracies were significantly more likely in attack than advocacy/contrast ads, and the logistic predictions of inaccurate ratings, are comparative/modelling results with no share reported. (5) The semantic network analysis of press coverage, the interviews and the National Annenberg Election Survey secondary analysis yield no misinformation-exposure share in the abstract.

rob.design: Multi-method design as described in the abstract only: a content analysis of 2008 presidential-election television ads matched to FactCheck.org and PolitiFact.com ratings; secondary analysis of the National Annenberg Election Survey 2008; semantic network analysis of press coverage of political TV ads; and in-depth interviews with scholars, practitioners, journalists and lawyers. Sample sizes, sampling procedure, coding protocol and intercoder reliability are not stated in the abstract. The dominant risk is stated by the author: the fact-checkers evaluated only ~30% of the ads, so the prevalence figure is bounded below by fact-checker coverage rather than measured on the full universe.
rob.item6_quote: Of all the English-language paid political ads that aired on television during the 2008 general election, just under 30% contained at least one inaccuracy based upon the ratings of FactCheck.org and PolitiFact.com.
rob.item10_quote: Of all the English-language paid political ads that aired on television during the 2008 general election, just under 30% contained at least one inaccuracy ... Among ads assessed, however, more than three out of four of the evaluated claims had some degree of inaccuracy.
